The Federal Government will repay a $500m World Bank agricultural loan over 20 years, beginning in May 2031 and ending in November 2050, under a financing agreement signed with the International Development Association. The agreement, obtained by The PUNCH from the World Bank’s website on Friday, provides that Nigeria will make 40 semi-annual principal repayments of 2.5 per cent each, equivalent to $12.5m per instalment if the entire credit is drawn. According to Schedule 3 of the agreement, “The Recipient shall repay the principal amount of the Credit” beginning on 15 May, 2031, and ending 15 November, 2050. The arrangement means Nigeria will remain responsible for servicing the agricultural credit until 2050, although the project itself is scheduled to close on 30 July, 2032. The PUNCH earlier reported in April that the World Bank approved a $500m International Development Association credit to boost Nigeria’s agricultural sector under a new programme targeting smallholder farmers, value chains, and food security. The funding would support the Nigeria Sustainable Agricultural Value-Chains for Growth project, also known as AGROW, which aims to improve productivity, strengthen market linkages, and create jobs across the country. The 29-page financing agreement obtained by The PUNCH covers this AGROW loan project. It was signed by the Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, on 29 October, 2026, while the World Bank Country Director, Mathew Verghis, signed on 16 September, 2026. Under Article II, the IDA agreed to provide “a credit, which is deemed as Concessional Financing”, amounting to $500m to support agricultural development. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. It also provides that the interest charge will be calculated using the reference rate plus a variable spread, less 250 basis points, subject to applicable ceilings and floors. The project seeks to increase smallholder productivity and strengthen agricultural value chains in participating Nigerian states. Of the total financing, $230m, representing 46 per cent of the fund, is allocated to performance-based matching grants for agribusiness investments. Another $229.5m, or 45.9 per cent, will finance goods, works, consultancy services, operating costs and training, while $40.5m is reserved for expenditure linked to performance-based conditions. The document explains that the matching grants will support investments in agricultural aggregation, storage, processing, logistics, post-harvest handling and market connections between farmers and buyers. The agreement also requires improvements in seed certification, fertiliser quality regulation and responsible land-based agricultural investment. However, participating states must satisfy several conditions before accessing the financing. According to Annex 2, states must adopt a responsible land investment framework through an executive order and establish regulations supporting a common digital farmer registry. They must also publish “a consolidated schedule of trade-related fees and levies for inter-state movement of goods” and reports detailing traders’ complaints and remedial actions. Also, states must publish policies linking support for agricultural cooperatives to verified commercial relationships with buyers. Failure to meet these requirements could prevent participating states from receiving project funds. The agreement provides that no withdrawal shall be made for payments to participating states until the Federal Government presents satisfactory evidence of compliance and executes the required subsidiary agreements. The World Bank may also withhold, reallocate or cancel financing linked to performance targets that are not achieved. Among the targets is the registration of farmers in a national digital registry, with basic and enhanced coverage targets of 40 per cent and 70 per cent, respectively. The agreement allocates $16m to this condition, with payments capped at $1m per participating state. Other performance-linked allocations include $5m each for improved seed availability and private investment in seed production, $2.5m for fertilizer quality compliance and $12m for responsible land investments. The agreement requires the Federal Government to establish a national steering committee and a project coordination unit within three months of the project becoming effective. It also mandates independent verification of performance targets, environmental and social safeguards, and periodic implementation reports. For artificial intelligence applications, the agreement requires risk assessments before deployment and prohibits uses involving mass surveillance, social scoring and discriminatory practices.
